﻿* Biomass Boiler
A biomass boiler generates steam or hot water by burning renewable solid biomass such as wood chips, pellets, briquettes, rice husk, bagasse, sawdust, and agricultural residues. The biomass is fed into a combustion chamber, where it burns with controlled air. The released heat is transferred through boiler tubes to water, producing steam or hot water for industrial processes. Unlike an electric boiler, it requires fuel storage, feeding equipment, combustion control, flue-gas treatment, chimney/stack, and ash handling. 
   


Field
	Value
	Process
	Steam/hot-water generation for dyeing, drying, sterilizing, cooking, food processing, textile processing, paper & pulp, dairy, chemical processing, agro-industries, etc.
	Temperature
	Typically produces hot water and saturated/superheated steam; steam conditions can range from low-pressure process steam to high-pressure steam above 300°C, depending on boiler design and application.
	Energy source
	Solid biomass — wood chips, pellets, briquettes, rice husk, bagasse, sawdust, coconut shells, and other agricultural/forestry residues.
	Efficiency
	Typically around 70–90%, depending strongly on boiler technology, fuel moisture, ash content, excess air, operating load and heat recovery. Well-designed modern systems can achieve higher values under favourable conditions.
	CAPEX
	Highly capacity- and configuration-dependent. A small industrial biomass boiler may cost several lakh to tens of lakh ₹, while medium/large systems can reach ₹1 crore to several crores+ after including fuel handling, storage, pollution-control equipment, installation and civil works.
	OPEX
	Dominated by biomass fuel cost, transportation and handling. Additional costs include electricity for fans/feeders/pumps, water treatment, ash disposal, labour and periodic maintenance.
	Lifetime
	Typically around 15–25+ years for the main boiler system when properly operated and maintained; individual components such as refractory, grate, feeders and control equipment may require earlier replacement.
	Space
	Requires more space than an electric boiler because of biomass storage, fuel conveyors/feeders, combustion equipment, ash handling and flue-gas treatment. Storage size depends on fuel consumption and desired days of fuel inventory.
	Constraints
	Biomass availability and quality, moisture content, ash/slagging, seasonal supply, transportation, fuel storage, grid electricity for auxiliaries, emissions regulations, part-load operation and availability of trained operators.
	Existing equipment replaced
	Can replace or partially replace coal, furnace-oil, diesel or natural-gas boilers when the required steam pressure, temperature, capacity and reliability can be achieved.
	Emissions
	Produces CO₂, CO, NOx and particulate matter during combustion. SOx is generally lower than for many coal systems but depends on fuel composition. Cyclones, bag filters, ESPs and good combustion control can reduce particulate emissions.
	Main by-product
	Bottom ash/fly ash, depending on boiler design and fuel. Ash quantity and properties depend strongly on biomass type.
	Fuel consumption
	Depends on heat demand, biomass LHV and efficiency. For example, a 1 MW useful heat demand using biomass with LHV = 15 MJ/kg and 70% efficiency requires approximately 343 kg/h of biomass.
	Main advantage
	Can provide continuous industrial process heat using locally available renewable biomass and can reduce dependence on fossil fuels.
	Main disadvantage
	Requires fuel logistics and storage, produces ash and combustion emissions, and performance can deteriorate when biomass quality is inconsistent.
	Key calculation :
For your project, this is one of the most important equations:
m˙biomass​=Q˙​useful​​​ / LHV×η
Where:
* m˙biomass​ = biomass consumption (kg/h)
* Q˙​useful​ = required useful heat (kW)
* LHV = lower heating value of biomass (MJ/kg)
* η = boiler efficiency


* Electric boiler
An electric boiler heats water into steam using electric heating elements or electrode/resistance technology submerged in water — no combustion, no chimney, no fuel storage. It's the direct electrical equivalent of a coal/oil/gas-fired boiler, producing the same steam output but via electricity instead of burning fuel.




Field
	Value
	Process
	Steam/hot water generation for dyeing, drying, sterilizing, cooking, cleaning — anywhere a factory currently uses a coal/oil/gas boiler
	Temperature
	Steam up to ~350°C, direct process heat up to ~400°C
	Energy source
	Grid electricity (3-phase supply required for larger units)
	Efficiency
	~99% — near-total conversion of electricity to heat, no combustion losses
	CAPEX
	Roughly ₹4–5 lakh (small, 100–500 kW) → ₹25–65 lakh (medium, 500 kW–1 MW) → ₹65 lakh–1.6 crore+ (large, 1–5 MW), scaling with capacity and pressure rating
	OPEX
	Dominated almost entirely by electricity cost — no fuel/chemical costs like combustion boilers, but tariff-sensitive
	Lifetime
	Typically 20–25 years (similar to conventional boilers), generally longer service life than combustion boilers due to less mechanical wear
	Space
	Compact — no chimney, no fuel yard/storage needed, smaller footprint than a biomass/coal boiler
	Constraints
	Grid capacity, 3-phase power availability, electricity tariff, grid reliability
